text: [INTRO MUSIC]
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Welcome back to The Influence Brief. I'm Sloane Bishop.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And I'm Victor Reyes.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Last episode we built the foundations — the influence map, currencies of exchange, the trust equation. Today we're walking into the room those tools can't fully prepare you for: the negotiation where the other side owns everything. The budget. The timeline. The template the negotiation happens in. Maybe your career. Because here's the thing nobody tells you about executive negotiation — the courses all assume a car dealership. Two parties, roughly symmetric, either of whom can walk out to the lot across the street. Almost none of your real negotiations look like that.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Almost all of your real negotiations are internal, and internal negotiations are asymmetric by design. You're negotiating headcount with the person who approves headcount. You're negotiating a deadline with the CEO who promised the date to the board. You can't walk out to the dealership across the street — the dealership across the street is resigning. So executives conclude, quietly, that these aren't really negotiations at all. They're rulings. You make your case, the powerful person decides, and your only move is to argue harder. <sigh> Which, as we established last episode, is the strategy of being right — and being right is not a strategy.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And the cost of the ruling mindset is bigger than any single lost budget fight, because rulings compound. The executive who treats asymmetric conversations as verdicts trains everyone above them that their asks are optional — soft asks, softly withdrawn, quarter after quarter, until the org's resourcing reflects everyone's negotiating posture instead of the company's actual priorities. Meanwhile the peer who treats the same conversations as negotiations — respectfully, without a single act of defiance — somehow ends the year with the teams, the timeline, and the mandate. You've watched this happen. You may have watched it happen to you.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: So the claim of this episode is that asymmetric negotiations are still negotiations — the power just lives somewhere other than where you're looking. Three tools today. BATNA and the reservation point, which is where your actual power comes from. Anchoring, which decides whose version of reality the negotiation happens inside. And calibrated questions — how to negotiate with someone you literally cannot say no to. Then the scenario: annual planning against a cost-cutting CFO who holds every visible card.
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

text: [MUSIC FADES]
chapter: INTRO: THE NEGOTIATION YOU DIDN'T NOTICE YOU WERE IN (3 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: The term comes from Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes — BATNA, best alternative to a negotiated agreement. And it's the single most misunderstood idea in the entire negotiation canon, so let's get the real version on the table. Your power in any negotiation is not your title, not your arguments, and not how much they like you. Your power is the quality of what you'll do if this negotiation fails. That's it. That's the whole physics. The side that can walk away more comfortably sets the terms, and both sides can smell the other's walking-away comfort with terrifying accuracy.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Which is exactly why executives feel powerless in internal negotiations — they hear "walk away" and think "quit," and since they're not quitting over a budget line, they conclude they have no BATNA and therefore no power. But that's reading the alternative too literally. Your BATNA in an internal negotiation is not leaving the company. It's the concrete answer to: if I don't get what I'm asking for in this form, from this person, in this cycle — what's my next-best path to the outcome? And once you frame it that way, alternatives start appearing. Descope and deliver the riskiest slice with the team you already have. Fund it from a different bucket — services revenue, a partner co-investment, the M&A integration budget nobody's watching. Wait a quarter and let the incident data make the argument for you. Take a smaller yes now that creates the evidence for a bigger yes later.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And here's the diagnostic we'd put on a poster: executives spend twenty hours polishing the case for their proposal and zero hours developing what they'll do without it. Then they walk into the room with one path — the yes — and the other side knows it instantly. Someone with no alternative doesn't negotiate; they plead. The counterintuitive move is that the hours you spend building your alternative do more for the negotiation than hours spent improving the ask. Not because you want the alternative. Because the alternative changes how you sit in the chair. You stop needing this specific yes, and people who don't need the yes get better terms. Every time.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Now, two clarifications, because this tool gets abused. First: a BATNA is not a bluff. A bluff is an alternative you announce but wouldn't execute — "if we don't fund this, I can't be responsible for what happens to the platform." The problem with bluffs at the executive level isn't that they're immoral, it's that they're checkable. Your CFO has watched you not-execute threats before. The moment a bluff gets called, you've converted a negotiation into a credibility incident — you've spent trust-equation capital to lose a budget fight. The test is simple: if you wouldn't actually do it with a straight face on a Tuesday, it's not your BATNA, and it should never leave your mouth.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Second clarification: the reservation point. Your BATNA tells you your best alternative; your reservation point is the line where the deal on the table becomes worse than that alternative — the point where you stop trading and switch paths. And the rule is: you decide it before you enter the room, in writing, when you're calm. Because inside the room, under time pressure and social pressure, you will rationalize. You'll accept the version of the deal that keeps the meeting pleasant, and three weeks later you'll be resourcing a commitment you knew was impossible when you nodded. Everyone listening has done this. The written reservation point is a letter from your calm self to your cornered self.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And notice what a reservation point is for an executive — it's usually not a number. It's a consequence you refuse to silently own. "Below eight engineers, the enterprise SLA commitment becomes fiction, and I will not let it become fiction quietly." The reservation point converts an unwinnable resource fight into a decision-rights question: fine, we can do the smaller version — but then the company is deciding to accept this risk, out loud, with names attached. That's not a threat. That's just refusing to launder someone else's decision through your silence.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Last thing on BATNA, and it's the part that separates the executives who have this tool from the ones who've merely read about it: your BATNA is not discovered, it's built, and the building happens between negotiations, not during them. Fisher and Ury are explicit about this and everyone skips it — improving your BATNA is the single most productive thing you can do before any negotiation. The exec whose platform work can be funded three different ways spent two years cultivating the services P&L relationship and the partner channel. The exec who can credibly say "we'll get the evidence and come back next cycle" built the instrumentation that produces evidence. Alternatives are infrastructure. Which is why the quarterly practice we'd actually prescribe is boring: once a quarter, take your three most likely upcoming negotiations and write down your current alternatives for each. Where the page is empty, that's not a negotiation problem yet — it's an infrastructure project with a deadline you can still beat.
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

text: [PAUSE]
chapter: SEGMENT 1: BATNA -- YOUR POWER IS YOUR ALTERNATIVES (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Tool two. The most replicated finding in negotiation research: the first credible number on the table warps everything that follows. Both sides adjust from the anchor, adjustments are always insufficient, and the final outcome lands measurably closer to whoever anchored. This survives expertise, by the way — experienced negotiators anchor each other just fine. So the question is never whether there will be an anchor. It's whose.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And executives who'd negotiate a vendor contract ferociously will walk into internal negotiations and accept the other side's anchor without noticing it was one. Because internally, the anchor usually isn't a number — it's the frame. The planning template that arrives with a column called "proposed reduction." The kickoff email that says "as we all tighten our belts." The moment you type into that spreadsheet, you have accepted that the negotiation is about the size of your cut. The negotiation happened in the template, before you said a word.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: So the discipline is: never negotiate inside a frame you wouldn't have chosen, and get your frame in first — or at least, get it in before positions harden. First credible frame, and credible is doing real work in that sentence. A credible anchor is ambitious with its reasoning shown: here is the outcome, here is the composition, here is what each piece buys. An anchor without composition is just a big number, and big numbers without scaffolding read as opening bids to be halved — or worse, as evidence you're not serious. The anchor's power comes from the other side engaging with your structure, because every minute they spend arguing inside your structure is a minute your structure is winning.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Let me make internal anchoring concrete, because this is the part nobody teaches. Anchoring internally means being the first to publish the one-pager that defines what the decision is. Before the CFO's template lands, you circulate: "Three ways to think about product investment next year — cost per committed roadmap outcome, risk of breaching the enterprise commitments we've already signed, and cost of the attrition we triggered last time we cut mid-initiative." Now the belt-tightening conversation has to route through your denominations. You haven't refused to cut — refusing gets you steamrolled — you've defined the units cuts get measured in. That's the difference between arguing about the answer and authoring the question.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Let me give you a timeline version, because the purest internal anchors are about time, not money. Two CPOs propose the same replatform. The first walks in and asks "how long do we have?" — and receives the anchor: "the board wants it by June." Dead on arrival; every subsequent conversation is a negotiation against June, and June was invented in a hallway. The second walks in with the anchor already published: "Replatforms of this scope run eighteen to thirty months industry-wide; here's the comparables table. I can compress to fourteen by cutting these two workstreams, and here's what each cut costs us." Notice she anchored on evidence about the world, not on her preference — which makes the anchor almost impossible to dismiss, because dismissing it means arguing with the comparables, not with her. When June inevitably surfaces, it now has to justify itself against her table. The number that arrives first with receipts becomes the burden of proof for every number that arrives after.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: One warning, because anchoring is the tool on today's list most likely to blow up on contact with power. Against a counterpart with real authority, an aggressive anchor doesn't get negotiated down — it gets dismissed, and you with it. The CFO doesn't haggle with your fantasy budget; she concludes you don't understand the company's situation and stops inviting you to the pre-meetings, which — episode one — is where everything actually happens. Under asymmetry, the anchor has to be ambitious in framing and impeccable in math. You want her checking your numbers and finding them solid, because — trust equation — every number that holds up is a deposit, and your frame only governs if your credibility survives contact.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And when you receive an anchor — because sometimes the template lands before you moved — the counter-move is never to negotiate small adjustments inside it. Haggling inside their frame ratifies the frame; congratulations, you're now debating whether your cut is eighteen percent or twenty. The move is to respectfully decline the units. "Before I fill in the reduction column — I don't think headcount is the variable we actually care about. Can I show you the same decision in terms of which committed outcomes we're keeping?" You're not fighting the anchor. You're changing the currency it's denominated in. Which — not a coincidence — is exactly the episode-one move, pointed at a spreadsheet.
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

text: [PAUSE]
chapter: SEGMENT 2: ANCHORS -- WHOEVER FRAMES FIRST OWNS THE MIDPOINT (6 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Tool three, for the hardest case: the counterpart who can simply decide. Your CEO. A founder. The CFO with full air cover. This is where BATNA thinking hits its limit, because yes, you have alternatives — but you can't exactly deploy leverage against someone who can end the conversation with a sentence. Chris Voss, the former FBI hostage negotiator, built his method for exactly this shape — every hostage negotiation is a power asymmetry — and his core tool is what he calls the calibrated question. Genuinely open, starts with "how" or "what," and it hands the other side a problem instead of a position. His flagship: "How am I supposed to do that?"
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And I want to be precise about why this works, because said wrong it's just passive aggression with a bestseller behind it. The magic is not the words. It's that the question moves the other person from evaluating your claim to authoring the solution — and humans defend what they author. When the CEO says "we need all of it shipped by June," and you respond with the counter-argument, you've made yourself the obstacle; the negotiation is now you versus the goal. When you respond with — genuinely, with real curiosity — "help me with the how: with these four teams, June covers two of the five commitments. Which two matter most?" you've made reality the obstacle and recruited the CEO onto your side of it. Same facts. Completely different room.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: The tone requirement is absolute, though. A calibrated question delivered with even a gram of triumph reads as insubordination-with-extra-steps — "how am I supposed to do that" in the wrong register is just "no" wearing a costume, and powerful people un-costume it instantly. It has to be deferential and unmovable at the same time: total respect for the goal, total honesty about the constraint. You're not resisting the mountain; you're standing at the base of it with the map open, asking which route they'd like to attempt. <laugh> The posture is sherpa, not lawyer.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: There's a second Voss idea that matters even more under asymmetry: stop hunting for yes, and make no safe. Powerful people are pitched at all day; their default defense is a vague yes that dies in the follow-through — you've all lived that. A clean no is actually more valuable, because a no is real information, and people relax once they've said it; it's the vague yes that kills you slowly. So invert your asks. Not "can you support the platform investment?" — that begs for the polite yes-that-means-nothing. Instead: "Is it unreasonable to protect the two squads on the enterprise commitments while we cut everywhere else?" Now the easy answer — no, that's not unreasonable — is the one that moves you forward, and it's a position they chose, which means they'll defend it in the pre-meeting you're not in.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Two supporting moves from the same toolkit, quickly, because they compound the questions. First, the label — naming the other side's position or emotion before they do: "It probably looks like product is defending its empire here." Said preemptively, it's disarming in a way that borders on unfair; the accusation they were holding loses all its energy once you've said it better than they would have, and what's left is the actual problem. Voss calls the systematic version an accusation audit — before a hard conversation, write down every negative thing they could fairly think about you and your ask, and defuse the top two out loud, early. Second: silence. After you ask the calibrated question — stop. The amateur fills the pause within three seconds, usually by softening the question into mush or answering it themselves. The pause is where the other person actually engages with the problem you just handed them; every second you stay quiet, they're authoring. It will feel like an eternity. It's usually about four seconds. <breath> Hold it.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: And under all three of today's tools runs the Fisher-and-Ury spine we should say once, explicitly: positions versus interests. The position is the demand — cut twenty percent, ship by June. The interest is the reason the demand exists — I need a credible discipline story for the board; I promised the anchor client. Under symmetric power you can fight a position. Under asymmetric power you cannot — but you almost never need to, because most positions are just one arbitrary way of serving the interest, chosen in about nine seconds, usually by analogy to whatever the board discussed last. Find the interest, and you can usually pay it — episode one, currencies — in a denomination that doesn't require the thing that destroys you. The powerful don't actually want their position. They want their interest, and they'll trade the position for it all day long, as long as the trade doesn't cost them face.
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

text: [MUSIC STING]
chapter: SEGMENT 3: CALIBRATED QUESTIONS -- NEGOTIATING WITHOUT THE POWER TO SAY NO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: The setup. Same CPO as always, two-hundred-person B2B company, and it's October — annual planning. The CFO — a year in now, credibility established, CEO fully behind her efficiency mandate — kicks off with a template. Every function gets a tab; yours has a prefilled column: minus twenty percent. Meanwhile, nothing else moves: the roadmap commitments to the three enterprise anchor clients stand, the CEO reaffirmed the retention targets at the last all-hands, and your calendar shows a thirty-minute "budget alignment" with the CFO in nine days. She owns the process, the template, the CEO's ear, and the timeline. You own... a strong feeling that this is impossible. <breath> Sloane — nine days. Go.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: First, feel the trap as designed, because it's elegant. The template does three things at once: it anchors the number, it makes the negotiation asynchronous — you versus a spreadsheet, no room to work — and it frames any pushback as a failure to be a team player during belt-tightening. Most of your peers will fill it in, grumble at their staff meetings, and spend the year delivering ninety percent of a plan with eighty percent of a team. That's the default outcome. Everything we do in the next nine days is about not being the default.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Day one is BATNA work, because everything else depends on how you sit in that chair. What actually happens if you don't win this? You build it out, in writing, three real paths. Path one: absorb the cut, drop the two lowest-consequence roadmap items, renegotiate one client commitment early — painful, survivable. Path two: absorb the cut on headcount but recover capacity elsewhere — kill the internal-tools squad's roadmap, move two contractors to the enterprise work, defer the replatform slice that isn't load-bearing until Q3. Path three: take the cut and formally hand the SLA risk upward. And now find your reservation point, and notice it's not a number. Somewhere around fifteen percent, the enterprise commitments stop being deliverable by anyone honest. Below that line, your position is: we can absolutely do it — as a named, minuted, CEO-owned decision to accept breach risk on the anchor accounts. You'll execute any option on this list without sulking. That's what walking in with alternatives means — and she will feel the difference before you finish your first sentence.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Day two, you anchor — which means you do not spend nine days preparing for the meeting. The meeting is the ratification event; episode one taught us where decisions actually live. Before the template's deadline, you send the CFO a one-pager: "How I'm thinking about the product budget." Three denominations, math shown. Cost per committed outcome — here are the eleven commitments the company has already made externally, here's what each costs to keep. Risk — here's the revenue attached to the three anchor clients and the SLA exposure at each cut level, in her units, dollars. And the honest one: here's the four percent I'd cut regardless, because it's real fat and she should have it for free. That last line is doing enormous work. It's an anchor with a concession built in — trust equation, self-orientation — proof you're optimizing for the company's math, not your org's headcount. You're not fighting the belt-tightening. You're competing to be its most rigorous author.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Then the meeting itself, where the tools change register — because in the room, she has all the power, and the only move that works is making her the author. She opens with the twenty percent. You don't counter. You say: "It's your call and I'll execute it — I need your help with one thing first. At twenty, we keep seven of the eleven commitments. Which four do we want to hand back?" That is a calibrated question with a spreadsheet attached, and watch what it does. She came to negotiate a number with a defensive product exec; she's now co-authoring a portfolio decision with dollars and client names on it — her actual medium. And here's the pivot that usually happens somewhere in that silence: she discovers that three of the four droppable commitments have her fingerprints on them, from deals she helped structure. The twenty percent was never her interest. Her interest is walking into the January board meeting with a discipline story that survives diligence. A fifteen percent cut with a rigorous portfolio logic she can present serves that interest better than a twenty percent cut that detonates an anchor account in March.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Notice, too, the accusation audit you ran in your opening ninety seconds, because it's easy to miss how much weight it carried. Before she could think it, you said it: "I know how this usually goes — product shows up to budget season with a hostage note about technical debt and a forecast of doom. I'm not going to do that; I brought the version of the cuts I'd make if I were you." Every stereotype she walked in armed with — the empire-defender, the sky-is-falling CTO-whisperer, the sandbagged estimate — you named and disowned in one breath, which is why the next twenty-five minutes got to be about the portfolio instead of about whether product executives can be trusted with sharp objects. <laugh> And when you asked the big calibrated question, you held the silence. Four seconds. She reached for the spreadsheet. That reach was the negotiation turning.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: And if she holds at twenty anyway — because sometimes they hold — the reservation point does its quiet work. No threats, no drama: "Twenty it is. I'll bring the delivery-risk memo on the enterprise accounts to the exec meeting so we can decide together which commitments we're re-dating — I don't want anyone surprised in March." You've made the cost of her position visible and shared, at the exact moment it's still cheap to modify, in front of the people who'd otherwise hear about it as a failure — yours — six months late. Notice nobody bluffed, nobody escalated, and every single move survives everyone comparing notes afterward. That was the bar we set in episode one. Asymmetric power decides who ratifies. It has surprisingly little to say about who prepared the decision.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Postscript, from a version of this I watched up close. The CFO took the fifteen-percent portfolio version to the CEO — as her recommendation, with her logic on the cover page, which is exactly what you want; episode one, the plan has her name on the slide. And in the January board meeting, the discipline story didn't just survive diligence, it starred in it: cut with a portfolio logic, commitments protected, risk memo attached. The CPO got something too, and it's worth naming because it's the real prize: a standing invitation into the budget process before the template goes out. That's what a well-run asymmetric negotiation buys you — not just this year's answer. A seat where next year's question gets written.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: SLOANE
text: Run the tape back: BATNA changed your posture from pleading to trading. The anchor decided which units the fight happened in. The calibrated question converted the person with all the power from your judge into your co-author. Her power never went anywhere — you just stopped needing it to move.
chapter: SEGMENT 4: THE SCENARIO -- ANNUAL PLANNING AGAINST THE CFO (5 minutes)

speaker: VICTOR
text: Homework, ninety minutes, before your next contentious meeting: write the BATNA memo to yourself. Three genuine alternatives if the answer is no. Your reservation point — the consequence you refuse to own silently — in one sentence. And the one-pager that frames the decision in your units, sent before their template lands. If you can't fill in the alternatives page, that's the finding: you've been pleading, not negotiating.
chapter: CLOSE: HOMEWORK & THE ROAD AHEAD (1 minute)

speaker: SLOANE
